title: Elder Nitaka: The mind is like a rock, Standing firm, unmoved. Toward agreeable things, The mind has no desire. Toward things that disturb, The mind…
content:
Elder Nitaka:

The mind is like a rock,
Standing firm, unmoved.
Toward agreeable things,
The mind has no desire.
Toward things that disturb,
The mind is not disturbed.
One whose mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come?

My mind is like a rock,
Standing firm, unmoved.
Toward agreeable things,
My mind has no desire.
Toward things that disturb,
My mind is not disturbed.
My mind is thus developed —
From where can suffering come to me?

title: “Monks, suppose a man is struck by an arrow, and then they strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the feeling…
content: “Monks, suppose a man is struck by an arrow, and then they strike him with a second arrow. Thus, monks, that man experiences the feeling of both arrows. So too, monks, an untaught ordinary person, when touched by a painful feeling, sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast, and becomes distraught. He experiences two feelings — a bodily feeling and a mental feeling. Touched by that painful feeling, he feels aversion. Because he feels aversion toward that painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling persists. Touched by that painful feeling, he delights in sensual pleasures. Why? Because, monks, the untaught ordinary person knows no escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure. Delighting in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling persists. He does not know as it actually is the origination, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding these feelings. Not knowing as it actually is the origination … and escape regarding these feelings, the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling persists. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is bound. This, monks, is called an untaught ordinary person who is bound by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is bound by suffering.”

title: “Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a…
content: “Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a defilement of the mind; thinks: ‘Ill-will is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons ill-will, the defilement of the mind; anger … hostility … hypocrisy … spite … envy … stinginess … deceit … fraud … obstinacy … impetuosity … conceit … arrogance … vanity; thinks: ‘Heedlessness is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons heedlessness, the defilement of the mind.”

title: Elder Mahākāla: One who does not know thus, Yet still creates attachments — The fool goes on, Experiencing suffering again and again. Therefore, one who…
content:
Elder Mahākāla:

One who does not know thus,
Yet still creates attachments —
The fool goes on,
Experiencing suffering again and again.
Therefore, one who knows
Does not create attachments.
I will not lie down
With my head broken.

title: "The monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and…
content: "The monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He drenches, saturates, fills, and pervades his very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that no spot on his entire body is not pervaded by that rapture and pleasure born of seclusion."

title: The Blessed One replied to Upasīva: “Mindful, not longing for anything, You will cross the flood. Abandoning sensual desires, free from doubt, Day and night…
content:
The Blessed One replied to Upasīva:
“Mindful, not longing for anything,
You will cross the flood.
Abandoning sensual desires, free from doubt,
Day and night see clearly —
The destruction of craving is Nibbāna.”

“One who is completely dispassionate
Toward all sensual pleasures,
Depending on nothing, giving up all else —
Freed completely, that is the supreme liberation.
There, that one abides,
And does not go on.”

“Just as a flame blown by strong wind
Goes to its end and cannot be measured,
So too the sage, freed from name and body,
Goes to his end and cannot be measured.”

“For one who has reached the end,
There is no measure by which one could speak of him.
When all phenomena are uprooted,
All paths of speech are uprooted as well.”

title: Venerable Ajita: “By what is the world shrouded? Why does it not shine forth? What do you call its defilement? What is its great fear?”…
content:
Venerable Ajita:
“By what is the world shrouded?
Why does it not shine forth?
What do you call its defilement?
What is its great fear?”

The Blessed One:
“The world is shrouded by ignorance.
Through stinginess and heedlessness it does not shine forth.
I say longing is its defilement —
Suffering is its great fear.”

title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is…
content: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

title: “Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will…
content: “Good, Māgandiya. I too have never seen or heard of such a one. But, Māgandiya, those ascetics or brahmins who have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful—all of them, having known as they actually are the origination, the passing away, the gratification, the peril, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, with craving for sensual pleasures abandoned and the fever of sensual pleasures removed, have dwelt, dwell, or will dwell with craving cut off and mind inwardly peaceful.”

title: “Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet…
content: “Monks, if a monk lives without ardor in his practice, though he may wish: ‘May my mind be liberated from the defilements without clinging,’ yet his mind is not liberated from the defilements without clinging. Why is that? It is because he has not developed. Not developed what? He has not developed the four foundations of mindfulness. He has not developed the four right efforts. He has not developed the four bases of spiritual power. He has not developed the five faculties. He has not developed the five powers. He has not developed the seven factors of enlightenment. He has not developed the Noble Eightfold Path.”
